items.title: Square of any number ending in 5
items.text: Take the number before 5, multiply it by the next number, then write 25 at the end. 35² → 3 × 4 = 12 → 1225. 85² → 8 × 9 = 72 → 7225.

items.title: EJOTY: find any letter's position fast
items.text: E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25. Count from the nearest one. R? T is 20, go back 2 → R = 18.

items.title: Since or For?
items.text: SINCE + a Starting point (since Monday, since 2015). FOR + a length of time (for 3 days, for 2 years). Both S-words: Since = Start.

items.title: Order of the planets
items.text: "My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos" = Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (closest to the Sun first).

points: BODMAS order: Brackets → Of → Division and Multiplication (left to right) → Addition and Subtraction.
× 5 is the same as × 10 then ÷ 2.
× 25 is the same as × 100 then ÷ 4.
To divide by a decimal, move the decimal point in both numbers: 72 ÷ 0.8 = 720 ÷ 8.
Learn squares from 1 to 30. They save time in almost every chapter.
tricks: × 5 → add a zero, then halve. 48 × 5 → 480 → 240.
1000 − 357: take each digit from 9, the last digit from 10 → 643.
Square ending in 5: n × (n + 1), then write 25. 65² → 6 × 7 = 42 → 4225.

points: To add fractions, make the bottom numbers the same first: 3/4 + 1/8 = 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8.
When multiplying decimals, count the total decimal places: 0.25 × 0.4 → 25 × 4 = 100 → 3 places → 0.100.
√ of a perfect square: use the last digit to guess the last digit of the answer.
× 11 has a quick trick (see below).
Always do brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −.
tricks: × 11 for 2-digit numbers: write the first digit, then the sum of both, then the last digit. 45 × 11 → 4 | 9 | 5 = 495. If the sum is 10 or more, carry 1: 57 × 11 → 5 | 12 | 7 → 627.
Square root last digit: ends in 1 → 1 or 9; 4 → 2 or 8; 9 → 3 or 7; 6 → 4 or 6; 5 → 5; 0 → 0.

points: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². Use it when two numbers are the same distance from a round number.
× 99 = × 100 minus the number once.
Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age): hunting, gathering, use of fire, rough stone tools.
Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age): microliths (tiny stone tools). Early animal keeping at Bagor (Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh).
Neolithic (New Stone Age): farming, polished stone tools, pottery. Mehrgarh (now in Pakistan) is an early farming site.
Bhimbetka rock shelters (Madhya Pradesh) have Stone Age paintings. UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Chalcolithic Age = copper + stone used together.
tricks: P → M → N = Palaeo (old) → Meso (middle) → Neo (new).
Microliths = Mesolithic: both start with M.
Neo = New things: farming, pottery, polished tools.

points: Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilisation: a Bronze Age civilisation, mature phase about 2500–1900 BCE.
Harappa: first excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921, on the Ravi river (now in Pakistan).
Mohenjo-daro: excavated by R. D. Banerji in 1922, on the Indus. Has the Great Bath and a great granary.
Lothal (Gujarat): dockyard. Kalibangan (Rajasthan): ploughed field. Dholavira (Gujarat): water system, UNESCO site.
The Indus script has not been read (deciphered) yet.
tricks: H before M, like the alphabet: Harappa 1921, Mohenjo-daro 1922.
Lothal = 'Lot of boats' → dockyard.
Mohenjo-daro = 'Mound of the dead' and has the Great Bath: 'M for Mound, Many baths'.

points: Simple present: habits and facts. He/she/it + verb-s (She plays, Water boils).
Present continuous: am/is/are + verb-ing, for 'now' (They are watching).
Present perfect: has/have + V3, often with since/for (I have known him for 5 years).
Present perfect continuous: has/have been + verb-ing (She has been studying since morning).
Verbs like know, like, love, believe are not usually used in -ing form.
tricks: He / She / It → add S. Think 'He Sings, She Swims, It Sleeps'.
Does / doesn't → base verb: 'He doesn't like', never 'likes'.

points: Simple past (V2) with yesterday, ago, last week, in 2020: I went, she ate.
Past continuous: was/were + verb-ing for an action going on in the past.
A short past action that interrupts uses simple past: I was cooking when the phone rang.
Past perfect: had + V3 for the earlier of two past actions.
After did / didn't, use the base verb: Did you see? He didn't go.
tricks: Did + V1: 'Did you GO', never 'Did you went'.
Two past actions? The FIRST one gets HAD: 'The train had left when I reached.'

points: Analogy = same relation. Find how the first pair is linked, then use the same link for the second pair.
Common links: use (pen–write), home (bird–nest), young one (cow–calf), worker–place, opposite.
Number analogies: try square, cube, ×2, n × (n + 1), +/− a fixed number.
Letter analogies: count how many steps each letter moves (A→B = +1).
Check all four options against the rule before choosing.
tricks: Make a sentence: 'A pen is used to write' → 'A knife is used to cut'.
For numbers, try n² and n³ first: 3 : 27 → cube → 4 : 64.

points: Number rule n × (n + 1): 5 : 30 → 7 : 56.
Young ones: cow → calf, dog → puppy, cat → kitten, lion → cub, horse → foal.
Professional pairs: doctor → patient, lawyer → client, teacher → student.
Word value: add letter positions (A = 1 … Z = 26): BAT = 2 + 1 + 20 = 23.
tricks: EJOTY = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 for quick letter positions.
Opposite letter pairs add to 27: A–Z, B–Y, C–X (1 + 26 = 27).
